newsitem.title: USA: US, Japan at odds on economic front before summit.
newsitem.headline: US, Japan at odds on economic front before summit.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent

The United States and Japan say they share concern about the recent weakness of the Japanese yen, but they do not seem to agree about much else on the economic front ahead of a summit here later this week.

The divisions -- on everything from the broad stance of Japanese economic policy to specific trade disputes -- are likely to be discussed Friday when President Clinton and Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto meet. But officials from both sides said they do not expect them to dominate the summit.

"The coming summit meeting...will most likely focus on the political side and security-related issues, but I don't deny that they will also discuss to some extent economic issues," Japan's Vice Minister for International Trade Hisashi Hosokawa told Reuters Tuesday.
The United States has made no secret of its concern about Japan's economic policy and has warned Tokyo repeatedly not to depend on stepped-up exports to fuel faster growth.
"We don't want to see a significant increase in the Japanese trade surplus," U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said last week.

That is exactly what some U.S. officials are worried might occur. They fear that a budget squeeze by Japan, including a recent increase in its consumption tax, will sap demand at home for the nation's products and convince its exporters to look abroad for sales.

It remains to be seen how forcefully Clinton will make that argument at Friday's meeting, but it is sure to come up at a Sunday gathering here of finance ministers from leading industrial nations, including the United States and Japan.

Vice President Al Gore raised the issue of Japan's budget policy at his meeting with Hashimoto in Tokyo last month. But Japanese officials said the prime minister strongly rejected suggestions that Tokyo take further actions to boost its economy if domestic demand slows in the coming months.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin received a more cordial reception when he met Hashimoto earlier this month. At that time, the Japanese leader agreed on the importance of domestic demand-led growth in Japan and the need to avoid a damaging rise in the country's trade surplus.
Japanese officials acknowledge that the April 1 rise in the consumption tax will slow economic growth, but they argue that the impact will only be temporary and limited.

They also highlight the benefits to be gained from Hashimoto's plan for massive deregulation of the Japanese economy and question whether the government could pump up its budget policy even if it wanted to.
Japan is already running a big budget deficit and further government spending would not be popular with the electorate.
Rather than focussing on the budget as a way to head off trade friction, Japanese officials have stressed the need to prevent a further rise of the dollar against the yen.

The weak yen -- it has depreciated by more than 50 percent against the U.S. currency over the past two years -- tends to bloat Japan's trade surplus by making its exports more competitive on world markets.
It also threatens to undermine Japan's already struggling banks by pushing down the price of their huge shareholdings on the Tokyo stock market.

Rubin has said he shares Japan's concern about a weak yen. But it is not clear what he is willing to do about that and, in particular, whether he is willing to sanction dollar sales by the United States in the global currency market -- a move that would be welcomed by Japan.

As Rubin never tires of saying, a strong dollar is in America's interest because it holds down inflation and interest rates here. It also helps support the U.S. stock market -- a fact not lost on the former Wall Street executive.

One policy shift that the United States would clearly not support to buttress the yen would be a rise in Japanese interest rates. Senior Japanese Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara warned last week that Japan's era of record low interest rates may be drawing to a close.
But Commerce Undersecretary Everett Ehrlich said that would be a bad idea, even though higher Japanese interest rates would make the yen a more profitable currency to hold.
That is because it would also dampen Japanese domestic demand.
